Giving Feedback on Implementations

How to tell an engineer that what they built does not do what it was meant to do — without telling them what to build instead.

1. Bengaluru, 11 February 2026

At 9.40 on a Wednesday morning, Ananya Bhatt sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Sopaan Money's office off Bannerghatta Road with a laptop, a printout of a funnel, and a problem she had been turning over since the previous evening. Sopaan Money is a seven-year-old consumer savings and credit app with 42 lakh monthly active users, most of them salaried people in tier-two cities who use it to park short-term money and to automate their bill payments. Ananya had been the product manager for the payments surface for nineteen months.

The feature in front of her was autopay mandate setup — the flow in which a user authorises Sopaan to debit their bank account on a recurring schedule, built on the UPI Autopay rails operated by the National Payments Corporation of India. Mandates matter to Sopaan disproportionately: a user with a live mandate has roughly four times the twelve-month retention of one without. In November the company had set an objective for the January quarter: raise the share of users who complete mandate setup, having started it, from 61 per cent to 78 per cent. Two sprints and about ₹38 lakh of engineering time later, Rohit Menon, a staff engineer with six years at the company, had shipped his piece of it — a retry layer that caught bank timeouts and silently re-submitted the mandate up to three times at thirty-second intervals.

The code was good. It was tested, instrumented, and it worked. And looking at the week's numbers, Ananya could see that it had moved completion from 57.6 per cent to 61.0 per cent, which was real, and which left the team fourteen points short of the objective with five weeks to go. Worse, she had a suspicion — not yet a fact — that the retry loop was itself costing users, because a silent retry means a user staring at a spinner for up to ninety seconds.

What Ananya did in the next conversation would determine two things. The first was whether the remaining five weeks were spent on the right problem. The second, less visible and more expensive, was whether Rohit would keep bringing her his thinking early, or start bringing her finished work late. She had watched a previous PM at Sopaan lose that privilege in about four weeks by saying, twice, some version of "why didn't you just cache it?" Engineering had politely stopped inviting him to design discussions, and nobody had ever said why.

2. The idea, stated precisely

Giving feedback on an implementation means evaluating a thing that has been built against the outcome it was meant to produce, and communicating the gap in a way that leaves the choice of remedy with the person who owns the craft. It has three moving parts worth separating. Evaluating is a judgement about fit between artefact and objective. Communicating the gap is an act of description — here is what I observe, here is what we agreed we wanted. Leaving the remedy is a deliberate act of restraint: you do not supply the fix, even when you think you know it, because supplying it converts a design problem into an instruction and quietly transfers ownership of quality from the builder to you.

The problem this practice was invented to solve is old and is not really about software. In any craft where one person specifies and another executes, the specifier's opinions about execution arrive with more force than they deserve, because they arrive attached to authority over the work's continued existence. The architectural critique — the studio "crit", formalised in the Beaux-Arts tradition and carried into twentieth-century design education at the Bauhaus — was an attempt to institutionalise commentary on work that improved the work without replacing the designer's judgement. Software inherited a narrower version in 1976, when Michael Fagan at IBM published the inspection: a structured code review whose explicit rule was that the reviewer identifies defects and the author decides the repair. Donald Schön's The Reflective Practitioner (1983) supplied the theory of why the author's reasoning matters — expertise lives in tacit moves the expert cannot fully articulate until asked. Mike Rother's Toyota Kata (2009) supplied the questioning discipline from manufacturing coaching, and Michael Bungay Stanier's The Coaching Habit (2016) named the thing most managers do wrong, the reflex he calls the advice monster.

From that lineage the modern product-management version condenses to three moves, in order: restate the objective, ask how they got there, bring evidence. The order is not decorative, and most of this page is an argument about why.

The sentence Ananya can say out loud without sounding like a management book: "Before I react to anything — here's the outcome I think this was for, tell me if I have it wrong. Then I'd like to understand how you got to this design, and then I'll show you what I'm seeing in the data."

3. How it actually works

The first move, restating the objective, is the one people skip because it feels like a formality. It is not. When Ananya says "this was meant to take mandate completion from 61 to 78 per cent by 31 March", she is doing three things at once. She is establishing that the subject of the conversation is an outcome, not a design. She is giving Rohit a chance to correct her — and he may, because engineers routinely absorb constraints during implementation that never make it back to the brief. And she is making the rest of the conversation falsifiable: once the yardstick is agreed, "the retry layer moves us 3.4 points of the 17 we need" is a statement either of them can check, rather than a matter of taste.

Restating the objective is not restating the ticket. The ticket said "implement retry on mandate submission failure". The objective was 78 per cent completion. If Ananya restates the ticket, Rohit has already met it and the conversation is over before it begins.

The second move, asking how they got there, is a reconstruction question, and its phrasing does real work. "Why did you build it this way?" invites defence. "Walk me through how you got to the three-retry design — what else was on the table?" invites narration. The difference in the answer is large. When Ananya asked, Rohit told her that the PSP's mandate-create endpoint is not idempotent below a thirty-second window, that he had wanted to show a progress state but the mobile app's mandate screen was owned by a different squad with a two-sprint queue, and that he had assumed — from the ticket — that timeouts were the dominant failure mode. Two of those three facts Ananya did not know. The third was a mistaken assumption she was in a position to correct with data, which is exactly the material for move three.

The third move, bringing evidence, means arriving with observations that have provenance rather than adjectives that have none. "The flow feels slow" is an adjective. "The p75 time from tapping Authorise to a terminal state is 47 seconds on 4G, measured over 8,100 submissions last week" is evidence. Evidence is checkable, which means it can be wrong, which is what makes it a contribution rather than an assertion of rank.

There are four steps practitioners leave implicit and that beginners therefore miss. The first is a private step before the conversation: separating the objective from your own mental picture of the solution, and noticing that you have one. The second is asking permission for timing — "do you have twenty minutes for this today, or is tomorrow better?" — because feedback delivered into the middle of a debugging session is noise. The third is explicitly agreeing who decides and by when, so the conversation ends with an owner rather than a mood. The fourth is closing the loop: coming back in two weeks with the measurement, whichever way it went. A team that never sees the follow-up measurement learns that feedback is a performance rather than a process.

4. The worked example

Here is the evidence Ananya assembled, for the week of 2–8 February 2026. Ten thousand users entered autopay setup. The arithmetic below is the whole of her case, and it is important that it is arithmetic and not an opinion.

Rohit's retry layer acts on the 1,250 timeouts, and recovers 340 of them — a 27.2 per cent recovery rate. Take it away and approvals fall to 6,100 − 340 = 5,760, or 57.6 per cent. So the retry layer is worth 3.4 percentage points, and Ananya should say so first, because it is true and because a conversation that opens by acknowledging what worked is heard differently from one that does not.

The decisive number is the ceiling. Suppose the retry layer were perfect and recovered every one of the 1,250 timeouts. Approvals would be 6,100 + (1,250 − 340) = 7,010, which is 70.1 per cent. Add back the 750 hard declines as though those too were solved, and the maximum reachable by fixing the approval stage alone is 7,760, or 77.6 per cent — still under target. In other words: every remaining unit of effort spent on the retry layer, however well executed, cannot reach the objective. That sentence contains no instruction about what to build. It is a statement about the size of a box.

The second pass: change one input. The 1,300 users who select a bank and never submit are the largest single loss after the approval stage, and nobody had looked at them. Suppose that loss halves, to 650. Those 650 extra submitters convert at the observed submission-to-approval rate of 6,100 ÷ 8,100 = 75.3 per cent, adding 489 approvals: 6,589, or 65.9 per cent. Now layer a perfect retry on top. Timeouts scale with submissions: 1,250 × (8,750 ÷ 8,100) ≈ 1,350, of which 340 are already recovered, so a further 1,010 arrive — 7,599, or 76.0 per cent. Still 2 points short, which tells Ananya something genuinely useful: even the two obvious levers, both taken to their theoretical maximum, do not reach 78 per cent. Either the 750 hard declines need a product answer, or the objective was set without this arithmetic. That is a conversation with her director, not with Rohit.

5. Nuances a learner must acquire

The implementation is not the implementer

The single most common failure is grammatical. "You built a retry loop that can't reach the target" and "the retry loop can't reach the target" differ only in the subject of the sentence, and differ entirely in what the listener does next. The second invites analysis; the first invites a defence of self-worth. Practise removing the second person from feedback sentences until it is automatic, then reintroduce it deliberately when the feedback genuinely is about the person, which is a different and rarer conversation.

The objective is not the ticket, and the ticket is not the spec

Three artefacts drift apart during a sprint. The objective is the outcome the business wanted. The ticket is what someone wrote down two weeks ago. The specification is what the engineer inferred while building. Restating move one means restating the objective. If you restate the ticket you have merely read aloud, and if you restate the spec you have picked a fight about memory.

"How did you get there" is an invitation, not an interrogation

The reconstruction question works when the listener believes you do not already know the answer you want. Two tells give the game away: asking it after you have already stated your preferred fix, and asking it in a tone that expects a short answer. The repair is sequencing — the question comes before your evidence and long before any candidate solution — and patience, because the useful part of the answer usually arrives in the third or fourth sentence, after the rehearsed part.

Not prescribing is not the same as having no opinion

Restraint is often taught as if the PM should have no view of the solution. That is both impossible and unhelpful; a PM who has thought about the flow will have candidates, and pretending otherwise is a performance the team can see through. The discipline is about ordering and labelling: hold the candidate until the objective, the reconstruction and the evidence are all on the table, then offer it explicitly as a candidate — "one thing I wondered about, and you'll know better than me whether it's silly, is whether we fail fast at ten seconds instead of retrying silently." The label does the work.

Authority makes musing into instruction

A PM's speculative aside is heard by a junior engineer as a requirement, because the PM controls what the team works on next. This asymmetry is larger in Indian workplaces with steeper hierarchy gradients, larger again when the PM is visibly senior or close to the founders, and largest of all in writing, where tone is lost. The practical implication is that the more authority you have, the later in the conversation your solution ideas must appear, and the more explicitly they must be marked as optional.

There are cases where prescribing is correct

The restraint is a default, not a law. Prescribe when the matter is legal or regulatory (an RBI directive on mandate disclosure is not a design opinion), when an error is irreversible or safety-relevant, when the engineer explicitly asks for your preference, and when the decision belongs to product by definition — copy, pricing, what the user is promised. Confusing "don't prescribe the fix" with "don't decide anything" produces a PM who is pleasant and useless.

Timing changes the act

Feedback before a design is committed is collaboration. Feedback after code is merged and in production is rework, and rework has a price that the feedback must justify. The same observation delivered at three different moments is three different acts, and a PM who only ever looks at implementations after they ship will be experienced as a source of expensive surprises, however gentle the phrasing.

What this method cannot tell you

Perfectly executed, the three moves establish whether an implementation serves its objective. They cannot tell you whether the objective was worth having. Ananya's arithmetic proves that 78 per cent is unreachable through the two available levers; it says nothing about whether autopay completion is the right thing for Sopaan to be optimising in February 2026 at all. That question is upstream, and no amount of good feedback craft substitutes for it.

6. How the practice shifts by product type and company stage

In consumer products the evidence is abundant and cheap: Ananya has 10,000 funnel entrants a week, so almost any disagreement can be settled by measurement within days. The risk is the opposite one — that the PM brings a dashboard to a conversation that needed a judgement, and hides behind numbers rather than saying what they believe.

In B2B and enterprise products the sample is small and the feedback loop is slow. A workflow tool with 140 customers may produce three relevant observations a month, so evidence is qualitative — a named customer, a recorded call, a support ticket with a reference number. The discipline shifts from statistics to provenance: not "customers find this confusing" but "Kavita at the Nashik distributor spent four minutes on this screen on 3 February and then phoned support." One named instance with a date beats an unsourced generalisation, and engineers know it.

In marketplace products the evaluation is structurally harder because an implementation usually helps one side and taxes the other. A faster seller-onboarding flow that skips a verification step raises supply and lowers buyer trust. Restating the objective therefore has to name both sides, or the feedback becomes an argument in which two people are correctly optimising different things without noticing.

By stage: in an early-stage company the PM and the engineer often sit two feet apart, the loop is hours long, and over-formalising feedback is worse than useless — the failure mode is ceremony. In a large company the loop runs through sprint boundaries, squad ownership and a release train, and the failure mode reverses: feedback that was never written down cannot survive a reorganisation, so the same three moves need a durable artefact — a comment on the ticket, a paragraph in the sprint review — attached to them.

7. Common mistakes, and the cheapest test for each

The smuggled fix deserves particular attention because it is invisible from inside. The PM experiences themselves as collaborative; the engineer experiences a series of polite directives. The counting test is blunt and effective: open your last five written pieces of feedback and mark every sentence containing a verb in the imperative or a construction of the form "can we just". Most PMs who do this exercise for the first time are startled.

The silent loop is the most expensive because it degrades slowly. Nobody complains. The team simply stops treating PM feedback as consequential, because in their experience it has no consequences — nothing was ever measured afterwards. The diagnostic is a single question asked over coffee, and the answer, if it is "I don't know, actually", is the finding.

8. What good looks like

Consider how the same twenty minutes would go in the hands of someone who has internalised this. Ananya books time the previous afternoon, tells Rohit what it is about, and shares Exhibit 1 an hour beforehand so he is not reading numbers for the first time under observation. She opens by restating the objective and asks if that is still how he understands it. He corrects her on one point — the ceiling for Q4 was agreed as 31 March, not 15 March — and she is glad of it. She asks him to walk her through the design, and learns about the idempotency window and the squad boundary on the mandate screen. She then puts up the ceiling arithmetic and says what it implies, which is not that the retry layer was wrong but that the remaining fourteen points are not behind it.

She does not say what to build. Rohit, who now has the funnel decomposition and nobody telling him the answer, says the thing Ananya could not have: that the 1,300 who abandon before submitting are probably waiting on the bank-list fetch, which takes 2.8 seconds at p75 because it is not cached, and that he could cache it in a day. They agree he owns the fix, that she will bring the numbers on 25 February, and that if the cache does not move the submit rate by three points they will escalate the target itself rather than keep grinding. Twenty minutes, one decision, one owner, one date, and a relationship slightly stronger than it was.

9. What Ananya decides

She decides to run the conversation exactly as described, and — importantly — to hold back her own hypothesis, which was that the spinner was killing people during retries. She holds it back not because it was wrong but because it was untested, and because putting it on the table first would have replaced Rohit's reconstruction with a response to her theory. It turned out to matter less than the uncached bank list, which she had no way of knowing. The second decision is the harder one: to take the ceiling arithmetic to her director on 13 February and say plainly that 78 per cent is not reachable this quarter through implementation quality, which is an admission about the objective rather than about the team.

What to learn next follows directly. The PM–engineering relationship is the container this practice lives in, and feedback is simply that relationship exercised daily; without the standing trust, the three moves read as technique. After that, backlog management and refinement, because a great deal of bad implementation feedback is really a symptom of work that entered the sprint without an agreed objective in the first place — and you cannot restate an objective that was never set.

Two questions to sit with.

First: think of the last implementation you reacted to badly. Can you write down, now, the objective it was meant to serve — in outcome terms, with a number — without opening the ticket? If not, what were you actually evaluating it against?

Second: when you withhold your solution, what exactly are you protecting — the engineer's autonomy, the quality of the eventual answer, or your own deniability if the fix fails? The three answers lead to different behaviour when the deadline is a week away.

The Skip That Nobody Asked About: Feedback After the Fact

Chennai, Sunday, 22 November 2026

The power in Siddharth Ranganathan's flat in Adyar had gone at half past nine, the way it did whenever the monsoon came in sideways off the Bay, and he had spent the first twenty minutes of the outage grateful for it. When the inverter caught, his laptop woke to the same three browser tabs he had been circling since Friday. The first showed that Adaptive Verification, the feature Deepstambh Signals had shipped in October, had lifted loan-application completion by 6.1 percentage points — the best number his product line had produced in two years. The second showed a spreadsheet from Toronto suggesting that the same cohort was defaulting on its first instalment more often than the customers it had replaced. The third was a Slack thread from 12 September, forty people deep, in which he had asked a question that he still believed was reasonable and that Purnima Deshpande, the staff engineer in Pune who had built the thing, had not answered in writing since.

At eleven the next morning there was a steering call with the founder, the VP of Engineering, and the sales leads for the Gulf and North America. Sid had to say whether Adaptive Verification would go live for the Dubai client on 1 January, whether the way it had been built counted as a deviation that had to be disclosed, and what he proposed to do about it. He had nine days before the disclosure clock ran out, one engineer who understood the code, and two sets of numbers that could not both be describing the same product.

1. Deepstambh Signals

Deepstambh Signals was founded in Chennai in 2015 by Anand Krishnamurthy, a former core-banking architect, and two colleagues from his TCS years. The name — lighthouse — was chosen for the pitch deck and stuck: the company sold the signals by which a lender could see who was standing in front of it. Its platform, Deepstambh Verify, sat between a lender's loan-origination system and the sources that could confirm an applicant's identity, income and obligations: the Account Aggregator framework for bank statements, the credit bureaus, penny-drop bank verification, video KYC, employer databases. By 2026 the company processed roughly 2.9 crore verification events a month for thirty-one lenders and marketplaces, and booked annual revenue of about ₹176 crore.

Two earlier decisions bounded what Sid could do in November. The first was architectural. In 2022, after the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions made lenders answerable for every data pull made on their behalf, Deepstambh had consolidated all consent capture, data retrieval and retention logic into a single internal service, the Consent Core, owned by a platform team in Pune. Product squads were forbidden from calling a bureau or an Account Aggregator directly; everything went through the Core, and everything the Core did was logged immutably. It had been the right call — it was the reason Deepstambh passed lender audits that competitors did not — but it meant that any change to what got verified, or re-verified, had to be scheduled against a platform roadmap that was booked to March, and that nothing could be quietly re-run after the fact.

The second decision was cultural, and Sid had supported it. In early 2024, after a flat funding year, the company removed a gate called Pre-Flight: a joint product–engineering review in which a PM and a tech lead walked through an implementation before it reached a customer. Pre-Flight had been slow, faintly ceremonial, and widely disliked; engineers described it as PMs reviewing code they could not read. In its place the company adopted written design docs with comment threads, on the principle that asynchronous review suited a team scattered across five time zones better than a meeting that only Bengaluru and Pune could comfortably attend. Cycle time improved by nineteen per cent in the first two quarters. Nobody measured what else changed.

2. The industry

The Indian verification market in 2026 was crowded and technically mature. Perfios, Signzy, IDfy, HyperVerge and Bureau sold overlapping capabilities; lenders ran two vendors in parallel and moved volume between them monthly on price and latency. The Account Aggregator network, coordinated through Sahamati, had made bank-statement retrieval cheap and consented; NPCI's rails had normalised instant bank verification; CIBIL and the other bureaus remained the spine of any credit decision. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made purpose limitation and consent freshness a board-level matter rather than a legal footnote.

The competitive pressure was not on accuracy — every serious vendor could verify — but on drop-off: each additional step a borrower had to complete, a video call, a bank login, a document upload, cost a lender between four and nine per cent of applicants at that step. Lenders had begun buying on funnel economics, and Deepstambh's largest Indian customer, a Mumbai-headquartered NBFC disguised here as the Mumbai lender, had made its 2027 renewal contingent on completion-rate improvement. Adaptive Verification was the answer: a system that decided, applicant by applicant, which verification steps could safely be skipped.

Deepstambh's foreign exposure was newer. A Dubai-based consumer-finance company, referred to here as the Gulf client, had signed in June 2026 for ₹9.5 crore a year, with a ₹4.2 crore milestone payable on a January go-live that included Adaptive Verification. A United States remittance firm was in diligence, its proposal from Rohit Sanghvi's New Jersey office quoting Deepstambh's October funnel results by name. Both markets had their own regulators, their own definitions of adequate verification, and no patience for an Indian vendor's process history.

3. What happened

The specification Sid wrote on 4 August was, he believed, precise. Adaptive Verification would skip the bank-statement pull and the video-KYC step for an applicant when two conditions held: a bureau score of 720 or above, and an employer present on Deepstambh's verified-employer list, the VEL, a curated set of some 41,000 organisations maintained by an operations team in Coimbatore. The target was a skip rate of thirty-five per cent of applications, because below roughly thirty the completion gain would not be worth the engineering.

Purnima Deshpande began building on 11 August. Within a fortnight she found that the rule as written produced a skip rate of nine per cent. The binding constraint was not the bureau threshold but the VEL: only thirty-eight per cent of the Mumbai lender's applicants had an employer that matched it, because the list had been assembled in 2021 for a salaried-lending product and never meaningfully refreshed. Gig workers, small-firm employees and anyone whose employer name was spelled differently in two systems failed the test.

What Purnima built instead was a composite confidence score: bureau score, bureau vintage, penny-drop name match, device and behavioural signals from the application session, and VEL presence as one contributor among several rather than a gate. Where the applicant's employer was absent from the list, the model treated it as missing information, not as disqualifying evidence. A floor was retained — nobody below a bureau score of 660 was ever skipped — and the threshold was tuned to produce a skip rate of 34.6 per cent, almost exactly the target. She wrote this up in the design doc on 29 August, in a section titled "VEL coverage and the confidence approach", six hundred words down a document that ran to nine pages. Sid left a thumbs-up on the summary line at 1:14 a.m. on 30 August, during a release week, from his phone.

The canary went out on 22 September and the full rollout on 6 October. The Diwali campaign ran from 24 October to 10 November, and the Mumbai lender, like every lender in India, spent heavily into it. Completion rose.   3. Reconstruct Purnima's position on 29 August. What feedback, delivered how and by whom, would have changed what happened next — and was Sid in a position to give it?

Giving Feedback on Implementations

Restraint belongs to remedies. It never belongs to evidence or to objectives — and almost every failure in this practice is a confusion of the three.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On the morning of 3 March 2026, Devika Rao was watching a screen recording for the fourth time. Devika is director of product at Sthiti Health Cloud, a Hyderabad company whose revenue-cycle software is used by 90 private hospitals across India to turn discharge summaries into insurance claims. The recording showed a medical coder at a 420-bed hospital in Nagpur working through a queue of charts on Sthiti's new coding-assist module, which since December had been suggesting ICD-10 diagnosis codes for each chart so that the coder could confirm rather than compose.

The module had been built to a clear specification, and it met it. Top-one accuracy on Sthiti's held-out test set of 41,000 charts was 93.4 per cent, against a spec of 92 per cent. Arjun Pillai, the tech lead, had taken four months over it and was entitled to be pleased. And yet coder throughput at the three pilot hospitals had fallen from 11.2 charts an hour to 9.6 — a 14.3 per cent decline — since the module went live. The module carried ₹2.8 crore of annual recurring revenue across 31 hospitals, and two renewal conversations scheduled for April were now awkward. What Devika could see in the recording, and what the accuracy number could not tell her, was that five of the six coders she had watched were coding each chart independently first and only then looking at Sthiti's suggestion to compare.

Six days later and 1,500 kilometres north, Farhan Siddiqui was in a different sort of trouble. Farhan runs the buyer experience at Chaturang Marketplace, a Gurugram two-sided marketplace on which roughly 2,840 small apparel manufacturers — most of them in Tiruppur and Ludhiana — sell to about 900 multi-brand retail buyers. On 20 January his team had replaced a hand-tuned search ranking with a learned model trained on eighteen months of order history. Nandita Bose, the engineer who owned it from Kolkata, and Tomasz Wierzbicki, the backend engineer in Kraków who had built the feature store, had shipped it cleanly. Buyer search-to-RFQ conversion rose from 8.1 per cent to 10.4 per cent; weekly gross merchandise value rose from ₹6.2 crore to ₹6.9 crore. By every metric in the project brief, it was the best thing the team had shipped that year.

The problem was on the other side of the market. Sellers with fewer than twelve historical orders had, as a group, gone from receiving 22 per cent of search impressions to 13 per cent, a 41 per cent cut — a cohort of 1,610 sellers out of the platform's 2,840. Weekly active sellers within that cohort had fallen from 61 per cent to 52 per cent. Farhan believed, though he could not yet prove, that the model had learned to rank on order history and was therefore slowly strangling the supply pipeline that the marketplace depended on for its next three years.

Both of these are feedback problems, and they are the same feedback problem. In each case a competent engineer built a thing that satisfied its written specification, and a product manager can see a gap between what was built and what it was for. In each case the product manager has an instinct about the fix — Devika wants to show one suggestion instead of three; Farhan wants a fixed exploration quota for new sellers — and in each case the instinct is based on less information than the engineer has. And in each case there is a second thing at stake beyond this decision: whether the engineer brings their thinking to the product manager early next time, or brings finished work late.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools that disagree about it

Giving feedback on an implementation is the act of comparing a built artefact against the outcome it was commissioned to produce, and communicating the gap in a form that transfers information without transferring the choice of remedy. The definition has three separable obligations, and the central argument of this page is that they carry different duties of restraint. You owe the builder a clear objective — restraint here is simply vagueness, and is always a fault. You owe the builder your evidence, all of it, including the inconvenient parts — withholding evidence is never a virtue and is the most common way this practice is misapplied by people who have learned it half-way. What you withhold, and withhold deliberately, is the remedy: the specific change you would make if the codebase were yours.

The problem is structural and predates software. Wherever one party commissions and another executes, the commissioner's opinions about execution arrive carrying authority over the work's continued existence, and are therefore received at a volume unrelated to their merit. Three traditions attacked this independently. In architecture and design education, the studio critique — formalised in the École des Beaux-Arts and carried into the Bauhaus in the 1920s — established that commentary on work should identify what the work does and fails to do, while the designer retains authorship. In software, Michael Fagan's 1976 paper at IBM on formal inspections made the same rule explicit and measurable: the inspector records defects; the author owns the repair; the two roles are never merged. In manufacturing, Toyota's coaching practice — codified for Western readers by Mike Rother in Toyota Kata (2009) — held that a supervisor who supplies answers destroys the problem-solving capability they are ostensibly building. Donald Schön's The Reflective Practitioner (1983) supplied the epistemology underneath all three: skilled practitioners know more than they can state, and the only reliable way to extract that knowledge is to ask them to reconstruct how they got where they are.

From this the modern product-management formulation condenses to three moves in a fixed order — restate the objective, ask how they got there, bring evidence — and to a fourth, unstated move, which is to stop.

That is where agreement ends. Four schools of practice hold genuinely different positions, and an experienced PM should be able to say which one they belong to and why.

The sentence that survives all four schools, and the only one worth memorising: "Here is the outcome this was for. Here is everything I am seeing, including the parts that argue against me. Tell me how you got here before I tell you what I think."

3. Mechanics in depth, with the arithmetic that justifies restraint

Expert practitioners do something before the conversation that novices do not: they separate, on paper, three lists. What they know that the builder may not. What the builder knows that they do not. And what they would do if it were theirs to do. The first list is delivered in full. The second list becomes the reconstruction question. The third list is withheld until the first two have been exchanged, and is then offered, labelled, or not at all.

Why withhold the third list? The usual answer — that it is respectful — is true but weak, and does not survive a deadline. The strong answer is an expected-value argument that can be written down.

Let pe be the probability that the engineer, given the objective and the evidence, selects the best available remedy, and pp the probability that the PM's prescribed remedy is the best available. Let V1 be the weekly value of the best remedy and V2 the weekly value of the typical second-best. In Farhan's case, take V1 = ₹1.00 lakh per week of incremental contribution and V2 = ₹0.40 lakh. Suppose pe = 0.65 and pp = 0.30 — the PM knows the market, the engineer knows the system, and in a question about ranking mechanics the engineer's hit rate is materially higher.

Engineer chooses: 0.65 × 1.00 + 0.35 × 0.40 = 0.65 + 0.14 = ₹0.79 lakh per week.
PM prescribes: 0.30 × 1.00 + 0.70 × 0.40 = 0.30 + 0.28 = ₹0.58 lakh per week.
Difference: ₹0.21 lakh per week, or ₹10.9 lakh over a year on this one decision stream.

Against that sits the honest cost of restraint, which advocates of the method almost never state: it is slower. Prescribing skips the reconstruction and the search, and in Farhan's case would have saved roughly two working days. Two days at ₹1.00 lakh per week of foregone value is about ₹0.29 lakh. So over a single week, restraint wins by ₹0.21 lakh and loses ₹0.29 lakh — prescription is ahead. Over a thirteen-week quarter, restraint is ahead by 0.21 × 13 − 0.29 = ₹2.44 lakh. The whole argument turns on horizon.

Set the two equal to find the threshold. Restraint pays when (pe − pp) × (V1 − V2) × T > delay cost, where T is the number of weeks the remedy stays in force. With V1 − V2 = ₹0.60 lakh and a delay cost of ₹0.29 lakh: at T = 1 week you need a judgement gap of 0.48, which is enormous; at T = 13 weeks you need only 0.037, which is nearly always satisfied. This is the quantitative form of a thing experienced PMs know in their bones — that prescribing is defensible in an incident and indefensible in a roadmap, and that the difference is not ethics but the durability of the decision.

Three second-order effects change the picture in ways the arithmetic above does not capture, and experts weigh all three. The first is capability compounding: an engineer who solves the problem this time solves the next one faster, so pe is not a constant but a function of how often they have been allowed to exercise it. The second is information return: the reconstruction question surfaces constraints the PM did not know, and those constraints are reusable across future decisions — in Devika's case the single fact she learned was worth more than the decision it informed. The third runs the other way and is under-discussed: restraint transfers cognitive load. The engineer now carries a problem they did not previously carry. If they are already at capacity, "I'll leave the approach to you" is not empowerment; it is an unfunded mandate, and mature PMs notice the difference by asking whether the person has room.

4. Conditions, stated as testable claims

The practice is not universally correct, and an expert can state the conditions as claims that can be checked rather than as a disposition. Five matter.

C1 — The builder holds material private information. Test: can the PM name three specific constraints the engineer is working under that are not written anywhere? For Arjun at Sthiti the answer is yes and Devika could name none of them — she did not know that the clinical-informatics advisor had required three visible code alternatives for NABH audit purposes, that the single-suggestion display had been explicitly rejected on those grounds, or that the audit log schema had been frozen in November. For Nandita at Chaturang the answer is also yes: Farhan did not know that the feature store computed seller-quality features on a seven-day lag, which mechanically disadvantages any seller with sparse history. C1 holds in both cases, which is the primary reason restraint is indicated in both.

C2 — The solution space contains more than one acceptable point. Test: can you, the PM, name two remedies you would accept? If you can name only one, you do not have a feedback problem; you have a decision, and you should make it and say so. Devika can name several. Farhan can name several. Where C2 fails — a regulatory disclosure whose wording is prescribed by the regulator, a payment flow whose steps are fixed by the scheme rules — pretending otherwise wastes everyone's time and reads as coyness.

C3 — The objective is measurable inside the loop's horizon. Test: name the metric and the date on which you will both look at it. Devika passes: coder throughput, measured daily at three pilot hospitals. Farhan half-passes: buyer conversion is measurable weekly, but the seller-side objective — the rate at which new sellers reach their twelfth order — takes a quarter to read, so his feedback must lean on a leading indicator, weekly active sellers in the sub-twelve cohort, and he must say explicitly that it is a proxy.

C4 — The cost of a wrong remedy is bounded and reversible. Test: what is the cost of undoing it, and how long does the undo take? A ranking change is reversible in an afternoon. A change to a claims audit trail, in a product subject to hospital accreditation review, is not, because past claims have already been filed under the old schema.

C5 — The relationship can carry a non-prescriptive question. Test: has the engineer ever disagreed with you in writing and been proved right, with no consequence? If not, the reconstruction question will be heard as a trap, and the correct first move is to fix that, which takes months and is not a feedback technique.

There are situations where the method is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading. During an incident, restraint costs money by the minute and hierarchy exists precisely to collapse decision time. When the engineer is junior and has asked directly for a recommendation, answering with a question is a small cruelty. When the "implementation gap" is in fact a product decision wearing implementation clothes — what the user is promised, what is charged, what is disclosed — the remedy belongs to product by definition and refusing to name it is an abdication. And when the evidence itself is contested, the feedback conversation should be suspended in favour of a measurement conversation.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product and platform. The hardest version of this is feedback that crosses a profit-and-loss boundary. When a platform team builds the shared component and a product team experiences the gap, the three moves break at move one, because the two teams do not share an objective: the platform team is measured on adoption and stability, the product team on conversion. The restatement — "this was meant to raise mandate completion" — is simply not the platform team's objective, and saying it louder does not help. Mature companies handle this by moving the conversation up one level to whoever owns both objectives, and the giveaway that a company has not solved it is a long, courteous comment thread on a ticket that runs for three weeks without an owner.

Two-sided markets. Farhan's case is the canonical one. An implementation that serves one side almost always taxes the other, so a restatement that names only one side converts a trade-off into an argument. The expert move is to restate the objective as a pair with an explicit constraint — "weekly GMV, without reducing the rate at which new sellers reach twelve orders below 17 per cent" — and to accept that if the constraint was never in the brief, the feedback conversation has just exposed a planning failure rather than an engineering one.

Regulated products. In Devika's world the audit trail is not a design preference. A suggestion that Sthiti display one code instead of three implicates what a hospital can show an accreditation assessor, and Devika is not qualified to judge that. Regulated contexts push practice toward the specification school for good reasons — but the corresponding failure mode is that "compliance requires it" becomes an unfalsifiable conversation-stopper. The discipline that separates strong teams here is insisting that every compliance constraint be traceable to a named clause, so that it can be checked rather than invoked.

Hardware plus software. Aparajita Instruments, a Coimbatore maker of point-of-care diagnostic devices, illustrates the timing problem in its purest form. Firmware for the March production run froze on 12 January; feedback on the firmware's calibration routine delivered on 20 January is not feedback, it is an expensive observation about the next run. When part of the system freezes and part does not, the PM must learn the freeze calendar as precisely as the sprint calendar, and must front-load feedback onto the frozen layer while deferring it on the mutable one. Teams that do not internalise this produce a characteristic pattern: thoughtful, well-evidenced feedback that arrives, every cycle, about eight days too late to matter.

AI-native products. Bodhak Labs, a Bengaluru company building an AI assistant for school administrators, changes the shape of move two. When the PM asks how the engineer got to this behaviour, the honest answer is often "I tried forty prompt variants and this one scored 0.81 on the eval set." There is no chain of reasoning to reconstruct, because the artefact was found by search rather than designed. Two consequences follow. First, the reconstruction question must be aimed at the eval set rather than the implementation: what does it contain, what does it fail to contain, and who wrote it? Second, evidence from the PM must be in a form the search can consume — a failing case added to the eval set is worth more than a paragraph of description, because it changes the objective function rather than the conversation. A PM who has not internalised this in an AI-native team will give beautifully phrased feedback that cannot be acted on.

6. Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The payload of the reconstruction question is the rejected options

Competent practitioners ask how the engineer got there and listen to the description of what was built. Experts listen for what was considered and discarded, because that list is where the private constraints live. The tell in the wild: an expert's follow-up is almost always "what else did you look at?" rather than "why this?". The obvious reading — that you are learning the design — is wrong; you are learning the boundary of the space, which is the only thing that tells you whether your own idea is new or already dead.

Provenance beats volume in evidence

A dashboard with a million events and no named instance is weaker, in an engineering conversation, than one recorded session with a date, a customer name and a timestamp. The reason is not sentimentality; it is that an aggregate is compatible with many causal stories while a specific instance rules most of them out. The tell: an expert brings both, and leads with the instance. Devika's four screen recordings from Nagpur did more work than the throughput chart, because the chart said "something is wrong" and the recordings said "coders are double-working".

Feedback latency is a design parameter, not a courtesy

How long after a change lands before the PM reacts determines how much rework the feedback can economically request, and therefore what kind of feedback is possible at all. Teams that treat this as a matter of politeness end up with a latency they never chose. The tell: an expert can state their own median feedback latency in days and has an opinion about whether it should be shorter. The obvious reading is that faster is better; it is not, uniformly — feedback at four hours on a half-built thing generates noise and anxiety, and several strong teams deliberately wait for a coherent slice.

Restating the objective is a lagging indicator of the planning process

When the restatement surprises anyone in the room, the feedback conversation has just diagnosed a failure that happened weeks earlier, at the point where work entered the sprint without an agreed outcome. Farhan's discovery that the seller-side constraint was never in the brief is not a fact about Nandita's model; it is a fact about how Chaturang writes briefs. The tell: an expert, on hearing "that's not what I thought we were doing", stops the implementation conversation and goes to look at the brief, rather than continuing to critique.

An implementation gap and a scope gap require different conversations

"This doesn't achieve the objective" and "this achieves a smaller objective than we agreed" feel similar and are not. The first is a quality question owned by the builder; the second is a commitment question owned by whoever agreed the scope, usually the PM and the engineering manager together. Conflating them produces the familiar bad meeting in which an engineer is asked to answer for a decision someone else made. The tell: an expert asks "was this in scope?" silently, before speaking.

Withholding a remedy has a cost, and someone pays it

Restraint moves a problem from your desk to theirs. When the engineer has slack and interest, that is a gift. When they are three days from a release and already carrying two incidents, it is an unfunded mandate dressed in coaching language, and it is experienced as such. The tell: an expert asks about capacity before choosing restraint, and will sometimes say outright, "I think the answer is X, I could be wrong, take it or leave it — I don't think you have room to search this week."

The channel changes the content

The same observation is a different act in a one-to-one, in a squad channel, and in a written review that a director will read. Public feedback on an implementation is simultaneously feedback and a status signal about the engineer, and everyone in the room processes both. The tell: an expert's public feedback is almost always about the artefact's relationship to the objective and almost never about a specific technical choice, with the technical conversation moved to a smaller room. The obvious reading — that this is political cowardice — is wrong; it is an accurate read of how an audience changes what a sentence means.

The flow is bidirectional, and the asymmetry is the diagnostic

Engineers give PMs feedback on their implementations too — on briefs, on prioritisation, on the quality of a problem statement. In healthy teams the volume in both directions is roughly comparable. The tell is not the presence of PM-to-engineer feedback but the absence of the reverse: a PM who has not received a substantive critique of a brief in three months does not have a feedback culture, they have a review process. The cheapest probe is to ask for one directly and then to visibly act on it.

Taste needs a comparison set to be legitimate

Some of the most valuable implementation feedback is aesthetic or experiential and has no metric behind it — an interaction feels heavy, a transition is jarring, an empty state is demoralising. Competent practitioners either suppress these observations as unrigorous or assert them as authority. Experts make them checkable by supplying a comparison set: three named products that solve the same moment, with what each does differently. The tell is that the expert's taste feedback comes with exhibits. Taste that cannot produce exhibits is usually preference, and an engineer is right to discount it.

7. How this differs by product type and stage, and where it does not

In consumer products evidence is abundant and cheap, and the characteristic failure is substituting a dashboard for a judgement. In B2B and enterprise — Sthiti's world — the sample is small, the feedback loop runs in months, and evidence must be qualitative with strong provenance: one named hospital on a named date beats "customers find this confusing". In platform and marketplace products the structural difficulty is that the objective is a vector rather than a scalar, and restating only one component of it makes the conversation unwinnable. In hardware the binding constraint is the freeze calendar rather than the sprint. In AI products the reconstruction question retargets from the implementation to the evaluation set, and the PM's most useful contribution is a failing case rather than a sentence.

Two claimed differences are, in practice, not real, and it is worth saying so plainly. The first is the idea that technical PMs can prescribe and non-technical PMs cannot. What matters is not whether the PM can read the code but whether they hold information the engineer lacks; a non-technical PM with four customer recordings has more to contribute than a technical PM with an opinion. The second is the idea that feedback is fundamentally different in distributed teams. Tomasz in Kraków needs exactly the same three moves that Nandita in Kolkata does; what changes is that they must be written down, and written feedback strips tone, so the invitation to reconstruct has to be made explicit rather than carried by voice.

Stage changes the failure mode rather than the method. In a twenty-person company the PM and the engineer are within earshot, the loop is hours long, and the risk is ceremony — running a structured critique on something that could have been settled by turning around. In a two-thousand-person company the loop runs through squad boundaries, release trains and quarterly planning, and the risk reverses: feedback that lives only in conversation does not survive a reorganisation, so the same three moves need a durable artefact attached to them. The method is constant; what changes is how much of it must be written.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Worked example one — Sthiti. The arithmetic settles what the accuracy number could not. The design's intended saving was 320 − 289 = 31 seconds a chart, about 10 per cent. The observed result is 375 − 320 = 55 seconds lost a chart, about 17 per cent. Thirty-one hospitals run an average of six coders; a 14.3 per cent throughput loss is roughly 0.86 of a coder per hospital, and at ₹4.1 lakh a year that is ₹3.5 lakh per hospital, or about ₹1.09 crore a year of cost that Sthiti has quietly imposed on its customers while charging them ₹2.8 crore for the privilege.

Devika's instinct was to show one suggestion. Had she prescribed it, she would have walked into the audit constraint and been overruled, expensively and in public. Instead she restated the objective — "this module exists to raise coder throughput by twenty per cent; it was never an accuracy project" — asked Arjun to walk her through the three-suggestion decision, and learned about the NABH requirement and the frozen audit schema. Arjun, now holding both the throughput decomposition and his own constraint, produced the answer neither could have alone: show one suggestion with the alternates behind a disclosure control, and write all three to the audit log rather than the screen. Audit satisfied; reading time cut from 55 seconds to an estimated 18. Whether coders then stop double-coding is a trust question that no amount of interface design settles in a fortnight, and Devika said so.

Worked example two — Chaturang. Farhan's harder arithmetic is a trade across two time horizons. The gain is immediate: GMV up ₹0.7 crore a week, ₹9.1 crore a quarter. The cost is deferred. Of 1,610 sub-twelve-order sellers, the historical rate of reaching twelve orders within a quarter was 19 per cent — 306 sellers. At the post-launch impression share it projects to 11 per cent, or 177 sellers: 129 fewer maturing sellers a quarter. A seller who reaches maturity contributes roughly ₹4.6 lakh of quarterly GMV, so the forward cost is about ₹5.9 crore a quarter, rising as the shortfall compounds. The honest conclusion is that the two numbers are close enough that the decision cannot be made on arithmetic alone — a conclusion Farhan must be willing to state rather than dress up.

Worked example three — the failure, at Vidur Payments. Sneha Kulkarni was a product manager at Vidur Payments, a Pune company selling a checkout SDK to mid-market online merchants. In October 2025 checkout completion on Android fell from 79.8 per cent to 71.3 per cent. Sneha had, in her notes, fourteen support calls in which merchants reported that the one-time-password field was not auto-filling after an Android permission prompt had changed. She had also read, carefully, about not prescribing remedies. So she went to Ritwik, the engineer, restated the objective, asked how the checkout had been built, and brought a dashboard showing p95 latency — and said nothing about the fourteen calls, because she believed that naming the OTP autofill would be prescribing the fix.

Ritwik did what any competent engineer does with a latency chart: he optimised latency, taking p95 from 4.1 seconds to 1.6 over three sprints. Completion moved by 0.4 points. Six engineer-sprints at roughly ₹2.1 lakh each is ₹12.6 lakh of direct cost, and seven weeks at an 8.5-point conversion deficit on about ₹11 crore of monthly processed volume is materially larger. When the OTP permission issue was finally found in December by a support engineer, the fix took two days and completion recovered to 79.8 per cent within a fortnight.

The instructive part is the recovery. Vidur did not abandon the practice; they corrected the confusion at its heart. The rule they wrote was one sentence: evidence is never withheld, only remedies are — and every feedback note at Vidur now opens with a section headed "what I know that you may not", listing observations with dates and sources, before any discussion of the artefact. Sneha's mistake was not restraint. It was applying restraint to the wrong object.

9. Failure modes, with early warning and the cost of a late catch

The costliest of these is the silent loop, because it decays without complaint. Nobody objects; the team simply stops treating product feedback as consequential, having learned from experience that it has no measurable consequence. By the time a PM notices — usually when an engineer stops pushing back — the repair takes two or three quarters of visibly closing loops, because the team is now testing whether the behaviour is real.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: the PM should never prescribe. In its strongest form this is not a claim about manners but about capability accumulation. Every remedy a PM supplies is a repetition the engineer does not get, and over two years the difference between a team that has solved four hundred problems and one that has executed four hundred instructions is enormous and mostly invisible in any single quarter. The evidence is indirect but real: teams with high engineer-originated change rates show better retention of senior engineers and produce more of the unprompted improvements that never appear on a roadmap. It would be wrong if pe were not in fact higher than pp in the relevant domain — which is exactly the case in a product where the hard knowledge is about users and regulation rather than systems, and where the engineer has never met a customer.

Position two: say what you think; peers do not perform restraint. The strongest version argues that everybody in the room already knows the PM has an opinion, that withholding it is a transparent ritual, and that the ritual costs speed at precisely the moments speed matters. Proponents point to high-velocity teams in technical companies where PMs are former engineers and the exchange is blunt in both directions without damage. This is correct where the peer relationship is real. It would be wrong — and is, in most large organisations — where the PM controls what the team works on next quarter, because then "just my opinion" is not a thing the PM can make true by saying it.

Position three: the framing is the problem; do not hand off. This position holds that feedback on an implementation is already a late-stage artefact of a broken process. If the PM, designer and engineer were in the room when the approach was chosen, there is nothing to review at the end, and the elaborate technique of restatement and reconstruction is a workaround for an absence that should not exist. The evidence is that most costly implementation gaps are set in the first two days of work and merely discovered on day forty. It would be wrong where scale, time zones or regulatory separation of duties make co-presence impossible — Chaturang cannot put Tomasz in Kraków in every Gurugram conversation — and it does not obviously survive past eight or ten squads.

Position four: feedback should be about conformance to a specification. The strongest case is that everything else is unbounded, that objectives are renegotiated by whoever argues best, and that a written contract protects the builder from a moving target. Regulated, hardware and multi-vendor contexts supply the evidence: these domains run on specifications and are not obviously worse at delivery. The position would be wrong wherever the specification cannot capture the outcome — which is most consumer software, and conspicuously Sthiti's case, where a module that met its 92 per cent accuracy spec destroyed the throughput it existed to create.

A fifth disagreement runs underneath all four and is rarely made explicit: whether a single vivid instance should outrank an aggregate. One camp holds that a recorded session is a sample of one and that treating it as evidence is how organisations chase anecdotes. The other holds that aggregates are compatible with too many causal stories to be actionable, and that the instance is what tells you which story is true. Devika's case is evidence for the second camp; a hundred PMs who rebuilt a feature because of one loud customer are evidence for the first. The field has not settled it, and the honest practitioner carries both and says which one they are leaning on.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives at a review with three questions written down. Someone who has internalised it arrives having already done the private work: they can state the objective in outcome terms without opening the ticket, they have listed what they know that the builder may not, and they have noticed — and named to themselves — the remedy they are itching to propose.

In the room, the difference shows up in three places. They lead with what worked, not as a technique but because it is true and cheap to say. They ask about rejected options rather than about the chosen design. And they are visibly willing to be wrong: when Arjun explains the NABH constraint, the master practitioner's response is "that changes my view", said out loud, which is the single most expensive signal a PM can send and the one that buys the most future candour.

Afterwards, they close the loop on a date they named in advance, whichever way the number went, and they carry forward the constraint they learned rather than the decision they made. Over a year the observable difference is not that their feedback is better phrased; it is that engineers bring them half-formed designs on a Tuesday instead of finished work on a Friday, which moves the entire practice upstream of where this page began.

12. What each protagonist decides

Devika decides not to propose the single-suggestion interface, and to bring instead the 375-second decomposition and the four recordings to a ninety-minute session with Arjun and the clinical-informatics advisor on 9 March. She also decides, separately and less comfortably, to write to her VP that the module's specification was wrong from the beginning — that a 92 per cent accuracy target was never a proxy for throughput — which is an admission about product management rather than about engineering.

Farhan decides that his first move is not feedback at all. He goes back to the January brief, confirms that the seller-side constraint was never written, and takes that to the weekly leadership review before he speaks to Nandita — because restating an objective that was never agreed is not restatement, it is invention, and Nandita would be right to say so. Only after the constraint is agreed does he take the impression-share decomposition to Kolkata and Kraków, with the explicit note that he has a candidate remedy, that it is probably naive, and that he will hold it until they have had a look.

Discussion questions.

1. Sneha at Vidur Payments applied a rule she had been taught and lost seven weeks. Was her error a misunderstanding of the rule, or is the rule itself too easily misread to be taught as a rule? What would you replace it with in a training programme?

2. Devika's module met every criterion in its specification. Who, precisely, is accountable for the ₹1.09 crore of annual cost it imposed on customers — and how does your answer change if Sthiti's engineering team had raised the throughput concern in November and been overruled?

3. The expected-value model in section three says restraint is almost unconditionally correct for decisions that stay in force a quarter or more. Name a real decision in your own team where that conclusion is wrong, and identify which assumption in the model breaks.

13. Going deeper

The PM–engineering relationship is the container this entire practice sits inside; without standing trust the three moves read as technique, and it explains why the same sentence lands differently from two different people. The software development lifecycle matters next because it tells you where the reversible moments are, and feedback delivered outside them is commentary. Agile in practice supplies the cadence at which feedback is economically actionable — and, read critically, warns against the mechanics-heavy version in which critique becomes a ceremony. Kanban and flow gives you the vocabulary for the capacity question that determines whether restraint is a gift or an unfunded mandate. The execution rhythm is where feedback becomes durable rather than conversational, which is what makes it survive a reorganisation. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing lets you price a remedy before you ask for it, so that you can tell the difference between feedback worth giving and feedback worth swallowing. And backlog management and refinement is the upstream fix for most of what this page treats: a great deal of bad implementation feedback is really a symptom of work that entered a sprint with no agreed objective, and you cannot restate an objective that was never set.

The Substitution Engine: Giving Feedback Before the Freeze

Bengaluru, 14 September 2026

At 6:40 in the evening, Ananya Rao closed her laptop lid halfway and reopened it. On her screen sat a dashboard showing that Vihanga Systems' new order-substitution engine had crossed its target metric with three days to spare before code freeze. On her second monitor sat a memo from a data scientist in Toronto showing that the same release, examined a different way, was quietly making things worse for the customers it was built to help. Code freeze for the pilot was Thursday, 17 September, 9 a.m. IST. Ananya, product manager for Vihanga's Order Cloud, had to decide what to tell Kabir Mehta, the engineer who had built it, and how to say it.

Company background

Vihanga Systems, founded in Bengaluru in 2016, sells order-management and inventory-sync software to sellers who trade across India's fragmented online-retail landscape — their own websites, the ONDC network, and marketplaces such as Meesho, Flipkart and Myntra. Where a seller on Unicommerce or Increff might stitch together inventory feeds by hand, Vihanga's software keeps stock counts, pricing and order routing synchronised across channels in near real time, and ships out orders through partners like Delhivery and Shiprocket. By 2026 it served roughly 1,800 sellers, carried an annual recurring revenue of about ₹96 crore, and had begun signing its first customers outside India, aimed at Gulf-based retailers who sell into the Indian market through cross-border storefronts.

The largest of these new accounts was a Dubai-headquartered fashion retailer, under contract for ₹14 crore a year, with a further ₹26 crore over three years riding on a successful pilot of Vihanga's newest feature: an engine that automatically substitutes an equivalent item when a customer's chosen size or colour is out of stock, instead of forcing a cancellation. Reducing cancellations mattered enormously to the client, whose biggest sales event of the year — the November "White Friday" season across the UAE and Saudi Arabia — was eight weeks away. The substitution engine was meant to go live for a limited pilot immediately after Thursday's freeze, then scale to the full campaign in November.

The situation

The brief Ananya had written in August was simple in intent, if not in execution: when a customer's exact size and colour were unavailable, the engine should look for the closest genuine equivalent — one size up or down, same colour family, similar price — and offer it as a one-click substitute. The acceptance criterion she and Kabir had agreed on was a "match rate" of at least 85 percent: the share of out-of-stock orders for which the engine found any qualifying substitute at all. She had also set what she considered a guardrail, not a headline number: the return-to-origin (RTO) rate on substituted orders — the share of substituted parcels a customer later rejects at the doorstep — should not exceed 10 percent, roughly what unsubstituted orders already ran.

Through most of September the match rate sat stubbornly at 78 percent, short of target, while Kabir and his two junior engineers in Pune worked through edge cases. On 2 September, with the freeze bearing down, Kabir widened the matching rule: instead of one size up or down within the same colour family, the engine would now accept substitutes up to two sizes off, and would drop the colour-family constraint entirely whenever no same-colour match existed. The match rate jumped to 91 percent overnight, comfortably past target, and Kabir posted the dashboard screenshot in the team channel with a relieved note that the engine was "green for Thursday."

What the dashboard did not show, Ananya learned on 10 September from Saanvi Krishnan, Vihanga's Toronto-based data scientist, who had been running a two-week pilot through test accounts that Reema Sundaram's Singapore customer-success team managed for early APAC users. Saanvi's numbers, laid out in Exhibit 1, told a different story: the substitutes the loosened rule was finding were often poor ones — further from the original price, more often the wrong size band, and rejected at the door far more frequently than before. Reema's team, meanwhile, had watched weekly support tickets tagged "wrong item substituted" climb from five to twenty-six. Ananya now had three days to decide what feedback to give Kabir, and how to give it, before the freeze made the loosened rule permanent for the Dubai pilot.

The options

Option A — Prescribe the fix

Ananya tells Kabir directly: revert to ±1 size, restore the colour-family constraint, and find another way to close the seven-point gap to 85 percent before Thursday. This is fast and unambiguous, and it protects the freeze date if Kabir can execute quickly. Its cost is that it treats Kabir as a pair of hands rather than the person closest to the trade-offs; it forecloses solutions Ananya has not thought of, such as a confidence-scored substitute with a lighter one-tap customer confirmation; and it risks the exact pattern repeating on the next feature, since Kabir has been told an answer rather than shown why his was wrong.

Option B — Restate the objective, ask how he got there, bring the evidence

Ananya sets up a short call with Kabir before Thursday, opens by restating what the feature was for — a substitute a customer would actually want, not merely a substitute that exists — asks him to walk her through how the team arrived at ±2 sizes and a dropped colour constraint under deadline pressure, and lays Saanvi's and Reema's evidence on the table without naming the fix herself. The upside is that Kabir, who best understands the matching code, is likely to find a better answer than Ananya would have prescribed — a tiered rule that only relaxes colour when price and size are both tight, say — and he owns the result. The cost is time: this conversation, and whatever Kabir proposes afterward, may not resolve by Thursday morning, risking the freeze date Ryan has promised the client.

Option C — Protect the freeze, monitor after launch

Ananya leaves the loosened rule as is, ships to the pilot on schedule, and asks Reema's team to watch RTO and ticket volume closely during the pilot, with a patch planned for the November scale-up if the numbers stay bad. This is the only option that guarantees Thursday holds and Ryan's commitment to the client is kept intact. Its cost is that it knowingly ships a release that breaches its own guardrail into a live pilot with a strategic account, on the hope that a fix arrives before the much larger November volume makes the same problem visible to the client's own operations team.

Questions for discussion

  1. What was the substitution engine's acceptance criterion actually meant to protect, and how did the 2 September change satisfy the letter of that criterion while working against its purpose?
  2. Read Exhibit 1 as Kabir might have seen it on 2 September, with only the match-rate number in view. What would have had to be visible to him, and when, for him to have caught the RTO effect himself?
  3. Compare Options A and B. What does Ananya gain by asking Kabir how he arrived at the loosened rule, rather than simply telling him what to change back?
  4. Given the numbers in Exhibits 1 and 2 and the Thursday deadline, which option should Ananya choose, and what would she say to Kabir, Reema and Ryan to make it stick?

A note for the learner

This case sits inside a simple but easily skipped discipline: when an implementation misses its intent while hitting its metric, the useful response is not to hand the engineer a corrected spec. It is to restate the objective in plain terms, ask how the team arrived at what they built, and bring evidence rather than opinion — then let the person closest to the code find the fix. Prescribing a fix, as in Option A, is tempting under deadline pressure and sometimes necessary, but it treats a judgement lapse as a knowledge gap, and it is usually the PM, not the engineer, who is guessing at the best technical answer. Option C is not really a feedback choice at all; it is a decision to defer the conversation until the evidence is harder to ignore, at greater cost to the client relationship it is trying to protect.

The defensible path here is Option B, compressed to fit the calendar rather than abandoned for it. Ananya should call Kabir on 15 September, not the morning of the freeze: restate that the feature exists to offer a substitute the customer would actually accept, not merely one the system can find; ask him directly how the team got from ±1 size with colour intact to ±2 sizes with colour dropped, since understanding the pressure he was under is part of preventing the next instance of this; and put Exhibit 1 and Reema's ticket trend in front of him rather than her own preferred fix. A two-day runway is enough for an engineer who built the matching logic to propose something better than a blunt revert — most plausibly a tiered rule that only relaxes on one dimension at a time, or a confidence score below which the customer is shown a one-tap confirmation instead of an automatic swap. If Kabir cannot land a fix that clears both the match-rate target and the RTO guardrail by Wednesday evening, Ananya should ship the pilot with the original, tighter rule and the lower 78 percent match rate rather than the loosened one: a smaller pilot that behaves as promised protects the Dubai relationship better than a larger one that does not, and Ryan can defend a modest, honest number to the client far more easily than an RTO spike discovered mid-campaign. Either way, the conversation with Kabir happens before the freeze, not after the numbers force it.
